data.sourceTitle: The Mughal Empire: Founding and Expansion
data.targetTitle: The Mughal Empire: Founding and Expansion
data.sourcePassage:
The Mughal Empire was founded in 1526 when Babur, a Central Asian ruler claiming descent from Timur and Genghis Khan, won the First Battle of Panipat against Ibrahim Lodi. Babur was an skilled military commander who used cavalry tactics and gunpowder weapons effectively to defeat a larger force. His victory gave him control of northern India, but founding an empire required more than winning a single battle. He had to win loyalty from local rulers, collect revenue, and govern diverse communities. Babur died in 1530, and his son Humayun struggled to hold power, eventually being defeated by the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri in 1540. Humayun spent years in exile before returning to reclaim Delhi in 1555, but he died shortly afterwards. His son Akbar inherited a fragile empire at just thirteen years of age in 1556.

Akbar proved to be one of the greatest Mughal rulers. During his reign from 1556 to 1605, he expanded Mughal territory significantly and built a much more organised and stable government. He created the mansabdari system, which organised nobles and military commanders by rank, giving the emperor greater control over the imperial administration. He also worked to improve land revenue collection through reforms associated with his finance minister Todar Mal. Most importantly, Akbar understood that ruling a diverse empire with a largely non-Muslim population required flexibility and inclusion. He formed marriage alliances with Hindu Rajput rulers, included non-Muslims in senior government positions, abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, and encouraged religious debate at his court at Fatehpur Sikri. By the time of his death in 1605, the Mughal Empire was far stronger and more stable than it had been when he inherited it.

questions.question: In which year did Babur win the First Battle of Panipat?
questions.modelAnswer: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

questions.question: What was the mansabdari system?
options: A system of religious courts
A method of building forts
A system that organised nobles and military commanders by rank
A way of trading textiles
questions.modelAnswer: The mansabdari system organised Mughal nobles and military commanders by rank, giving the emperor greater control over the imperial administration.

questions.question: Why did Akbar abolish the jizya and form alliances with Rajput rulers?
options: Because he was not a Muslim and did not believe in the tax
Because he understood that ruling a diverse empire with a largely non-Muslim population required flexibility and inclusion
Because the Rajputs were more powerful than the Mughals
Because European trading companies demanded these changes
questions.modelAnswer: Akbar abolished the jizya and formed alliances with Rajput rulers because he understood that ruling a diverse empire with a largely non-Muslim population required flexibility and inclusion. Without the cooperation of powerful Hindu groups and non-Muslim communities, governing such a vast territory would have been much harder.

questions.question: What does Humayun's loss of power and later recovery suggest about the early Mughal Empire?
options: That the Mughal Empire was always very stable and powerful
That winning a battle was enough to secure an empire permanently
That the early Mughal Empire was fragile and required constant effort to maintain
That Humayun was a stronger ruler than Babur
questions.modelAnswer: Humayun's defeat by Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and subsequent years in exile show that the early Mughal Empire was fragile. Simply winning the Battle of Panipat was not enough to secure permanent control. Rulers had to maintain military strength, win loyalty from local elites, and govern effectively. The empire could be lost as well as won.

data.sourceTitle: Akbar the Great and the Age of Tolerance
data.targetTitle: Akbar the Great and the Age of Tolerance
data.sourcePassage:
Akbar is often described as the greatest of all the Mughal emperors, and historians have long debated the reasons for his success. His religious policies have attracted particular attention. Mughal India was home to Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, Christians, and many others. Akbar's approach was unusually inclusive for an early modern ruler. He abolished the jizya, a tax that had been imposed on non-Muslim subjects, and he created the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri — a 'House of Worship' where scholars from different faiths gathered to debate religion and ideas. He appointed Hindus to senior positions in government and military command, and he formed marriage alliances with Hindu Rajput rulers, bringing their loyalty into the Mughal system.

Historians debate whether Akbar's tolerance was driven by genuine belief or by practical politics. Some argue that he was a remarkably open-minded thinker who genuinely sought religious truth. Others point out that ruling a huge empire in which the majority of people were not Muslim made inclusion a political necessity — without the cooperation of Hindu elites, stable governance would have been much harder to achieve. Most historians accept that both were probably true: Akbar may have been personally curious about religion, and he certainly understood that inclusion was politically useful.

Akbar's court was also a centre of art and culture. Under his patronage, miniature painting flourished, translation projects brought Persian and Sanskrit texts into new languages, and architecture blended Central Asian, Persian, and Indian styles. Fatehpur Sikri itself, built in the 1570s, is a remarkable monument to Akbar's power and cultural ambition. By the time he died in 1605, Akbar had transformed the Mughal Empire from an unstable conquest into a sophisticated, powerful state.

questions.question: What was the Ibadat Khana?
options: A military fort at Fatehpur Sikri
A 'House of Worship' where scholars from different faiths debated ideas
A type of tax on non-Muslim subjects
A translation project at Akbar's court
questions.modelAnswer: The Ibadat Khana was a 'House of Worship' created by Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars from different religious traditions gathered to debate religion and ideas.

questions.question: Name one way Akbar showed religious inclusion in his government.
options: He built mosques in every province
He made Islam compulsory for all officials
He appointed Hindus to senior government and military positions
He abolished all religions except Islam
questions.modelAnswer: Akbar showed religious inclusion by appointing Hindus to senior positions in government and military command, and by abolishing the jizya tax on non-Muslim subjects.

questions.question: What are the two different interpretations historians give for why Akbar had inclusive religious policies?
options: Some say he was forced to by the Rajputs; others say European traders required it
Some say it was genuine religious belief; others say it was practical political necessity
Some say it was because of the jizya revenues; others say it was to please the Rajputs
Some say it happened by accident; others say Akbar copied Persian rulers
questions.modelAnswer: One interpretation is that Akbar was genuinely curious and open-minded about religion. The other interpretation is that including non-Muslims was a political necessity in an empire where the majority of people were not Muslim. Most historians think both were probably true.

questions.question: How does the passage suggest we should evaluate Akbar as a historical figure?
options: We should praise him as perfectly tolerant and equal to modern democratic leaders
We should condemn him because he was only interested in power, not religion
We should recognise both his genuine qualities and the political context that shaped his choices, avoiding simplistic labels
We should focus only on his architectural achievements
questions.modelAnswer: The passage suggests we should evaluate Akbar with nuance — recognising both the genuine qualities he may have had (intellectual curiosity, openness to different faiths) and the political context that shaped his choices (the practical need to govern a diverse empire). We should avoid both uncritical praise ('he was like a modern democrat') and dismissiveness ('it was all political calculation').

data.sourceTitle: The Decline of the Mughal Empire
data.targetTitle: The Decline of the Mughal Empire
data.sourcePassage:
The Mughal Empire reached its greatest territorial extent under Aurangzeb, who ruled from 1658 to 1707. He expanded Mughal power deep into the Deccan plateau in central and southern India, defeating rival powers and establishing the largest Mughal Empire ever. Yet this period of greatest size was also the beginning of serious decline. The Deccan campaigns were enormously expensive and lasted for decades. They stretched the army, exhausted the treasury, and made it harder to govern the rest of the empire effectively. Aurangzeb spent the last years of his long reign in the Deccan rather than at court, which weakened central authority.

Aurangzeb is one of the most controversial of all Mughal rulers. He reintroduced the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1679, which Akbar had abolished. He had conflicts with some Rajput groups and with the growing Maratha confederacy in the Deccan. Some historians argue that his stricter Islamic policies damaged the unity that Akbar had built. Others point out that he continued to employ many Hindu officials, and that the problems he faced — regional resistance, succession rivalries, expensive wars — were not simply caused by religious policy. Good history avoids simple labels of 'good' or 'bad' ruler.

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, Mughal power fragmented quickly. Regional rulers became more independent, succession wars weakened the central dynasty, and European trading companies — especially the English East India Company — took advantage of political instability. The Battle of Plassey in 1757 marked the Company's decisive entry into Indian politics. The last Mughal emperor was deposed in 1857. The empire that Babur had built in 1526 had lasted over three centuries, leaving an extraordinary cultural, architectural, and administrative legacy.

questions.question: Which Mughal emperor expanded the empire to its greatest territorial extent?
options: Akbar
Shah Jahan
Aurangzeb
Babur
questions.modelAnswer: Aurangzeb expanded the Mughal Empire to its greatest territorial extent during his reign from 1658 to 1707.

questions.question: What tax did Aurangzeb reintroduce in 1679 that Akbar had abolished?
options: The jagir
The jizya
The zamindar levy
The subah tax
questions.modelAnswer: Aurangzeb reintroduced the jizya, a tax on non-Muslim subjects, in 1679. This was a reversal of Akbar's policy of abolishing it.

questions.question: Why does the passage say 'the period of greatest size was also the beginning of serious decline'?
options: Because Aurangzeb refused to trade with European companies
Because expanding the empire created enormous military and financial burdens that weakened the Mughals
Because other rulers were stronger than Aurangzeb
Because the Taj Mahal cost too much money to maintain
questions.modelAnswer: The Deccan campaigns that expanded the empire were enormously expensive and lasted decades, stretching the army and exhausting the treasury. A larger empire was harder and more costly to govern effectively. This shows that military expansion does not always make a state stronger — sometimes it creates pressures that lead to weakness.

questions.question: What is the most balanced interpretation of Aurangzeb's role in Mughal decline, according to the passage?
options: Aurangzeb was solely responsible for the decline because of his religious policies
Aurangzeb had no responsibility for decline since the problems were inherited
Aurangzeb's expansion and policies created significant pressures, but decline also came from wider structural problems like succession rivalry and regional resistance
Aurangzeb's decline was entirely caused by the East India Company
questions.modelAnswer: The most balanced interpretation is that Aurangzeb's policies and military campaigns created significant new pressures — particularly the ruinously expensive Deccan wars and tensions caused by reintroducing the jizya. However, decline also came from wider structural problems including succession rivalries, regional resistance, and the growing power of European trading companies. Good history avoids simple 'good ruler/bad ruler' labels.
